record.original_question: Can one develop a formal theoretical analysis and an agreed set of measures for comparing the performance of different metaheuristic algorithms, beyond commonly used empirical measures such as absolute objective value and number of function evaluations?

evidence.quote: Another important question is about the performance comparison. At the moment, there is no agreed measure for comparing performance of different algorithms, though the absolute objective value and the number of function evaluations are two widely used measures. However, a formal theoretical analysis is yet to be developed.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A metaheuristic algorithm is a (typically stochastic) iterative procedure designed to approximately solve optimization problems of the form minimize f(x) over x in a domain D, by maintaining and updating candidate solutions according to a fixed set of rules and control parameters. Common examples include simulated annealing, genetic algorithms, particle swarm optimization, differential evolution, and ant colony optimization. In current practice, two algorithms A and B are usually compared empirically by running each on a chosen benchmark instance multiple times and reporting (i) the absolute best objective value f(x*) found, and (ii) the number of objective-function evaluations used.

Develop a formal theoretical framework for comparing the performance of metaheuristic algorithms that goes beyond such purely empirical reporting. Concretely:

1. Propose a rigorously defined and universally applicable set of performance measures M_1, ..., M_k for stochastic optimization heuristics that jointly capture solution quality, computational cost, convergence behaviour, robustness to parameter choices, and dependence on problem structure.

2. Provide a mathematical formulation (for example, in terms of a probability space governing the randomness of the algorithm and a class of admissible objective functions f : D -> R) under which these measures are well-defined random variables or functionals, and prove their basic properties (existence, invariance under reasonable transformations, comparability across algorithms).

3. Using this framework, derive theorems that allow one to assert, in a precise sense, that one metaheuristic algorithm outperforms another on a specified class of optimization problems, and establish when such a comparison is consistent across problem classes.

The task is to determine whether such a formal theoretical analysis, together with an agreed canonical set of comparison measures, can be developed.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent surveys and reviews (2020–2025) on metaheuristic performance assessment continue to emphasize the lack of a universally agreed theoretical framework or canonical measure set. Various partial frameworks (Monte Carlo-based assessment, efficiency vs. effectiveness decompositions, multi-objective indicators like IGD, statistical testing) have been proposed, but the field still relies primarily on empirical benchmarking and there is no consensus formal theory for cross-algorithm comparison. The problem appears still open.

status_evidence.title: Performance assessment of the metaheuristic optimization algorithms: an exhaustive review
status_evidence.snippet: Review of performance assessment approaches for metaheuristics, noting reliance on empirical and statistical comparison.
status_evidence.claim: No single agreed-upon theoretical framework; review enumerates many ad hoc measures.

status_evidence.title: An exhaustive review of the metaheuristic algorithms for search and optimization: taxonomy, applications, and open challenges
status_evidence.snippet: Lists open challenges including unified theoretical analysis and standardized comparison measures.
status_evidence.claim: Standardized theoretical performance comparison remains an open challenge.

status_evidence.title: Performance Assessment of Metaheuristic Algorithms for Structural Optimization
status_evidence.snippet: Proposes a Monte Carlo–based probabilistic assessment incorporating control parameter randomness.
status_evidence.claim: Partial probabilistic frameworks exist but are not universally adopted.
